It's all about trying to fix or hide how wrong I think I look before anyone else can see me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any periods in your life where you didn't care about how your face or jawline looked, or has this concern been constant and persistent over time?\n\nPatient: I've always had some self-consciousness about my looks, but it has become much more constant and intense recently. It got significantly worse when my soccer teammates started posting high-resolution photos and videos of us online. Now, seeing those images has made me fixate on my crooked face and jawline almost constantly.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your excessive checking and rechecking behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing a specific, catastrophic outcome, such as being ridiculed or rejected by others, or are they more focused on achieving a sense of perfection or symmetry in your appearance?\n\nPatient: It’s actually a mix of both. I’m highly focused on trying to make my face look \"right\" and less crooked, but my ultimate fear is having other people see me looking so \"messed up.\" If I can't get it to look right in the mirror, I end up canceling my plans because I just can't let anyone see me that way.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your behaviors are mainly focused on your appearance concerns, but can you think of any times when you've had repetitive thoughts or urges that aren't related to how you look, such as fears of contamination, harm, or needing things to be perfectly arranged?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never had any of those fears about germs, harm, or needing things to be perfectly arranged. My worries are completely and strictly focused on how crooked my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel emotionally when you're unable to check or fix your appearance, and does it feel like you're trying to reduce anxiety or prevent something bad from happening when you do check?\n\nPatient: If I can't check or fix my appearance, I feel incredibly anxious and uncomfortable because I feel like I absolutely cannot let anyone see me looking \"wrong.\" The checking is my way of trying to reduce that panic and make sure my face looks okay. My worries are completely and strictly focused on how crooked my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel emotionally when you're unable to check or fix your appearance, and does it feel like you're trying to reduce anxiety or prevent something bad from happening when you do check?\n\nPatient: If I can't check or fix my appearance, I feel incredibly anxious and uncomfortable because I feel like I absolutely cannot let anyone see me looking \"wrong.\" The checking is my way of trying to reduce that panic and make sure my face looks okay. If I can't get it right, the distress of being seen from a crooked angle is so intense that I'll just cancel my plans and stay home.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your preoccupation with your appearance, such as the perceived crookedness of your face, feels like an intrusive thought that you try to ignore or suppress, or is it more of a voluntary concern that you feel is justified and important to address?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to describe it like that. It just feels incredibly overwhelming and it's really hard to stop thinking about, no matter what I do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that these thoughts about your face being crooked are popping into your mind without you wanting them to, or are they more something you deliberately think about because you're concerned about your appearance?\n\nPatient: They definitely pop into my head automatically without me wanting them to. Even if I try to focus on something else, my mind just goes right back to worrying about how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: You've consistently mentioned that your concerns and behaviors are strictly about your appearance, but can you think of any situation or time where you felt compelled to repeat a behavior or thought that wasn't related to how you look, even if it seems minor or insignificant?\n\nPatient: No, I really can't think of any repetitive behaviors or thoughts that aren't about how I look. All of these habits and worries are strictly tied to my appearance and trying to hide my face.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered that your excessive focus on your appearance might be a symptom of a broader issue, rather than just a concern about how you look, and if so, how do you think that might relate to your overall well-being?\n\nPatient: While the crookedness of my face feels completely real to me, even though my friends say they don't see anything, I am starting to realize that the sheer amount of time and energy I spend worrying about it has become a massive, overwhelming problem of its own. It has severely damaged my well-being by causing me to miss work shifts, avoid my friends, and stop doing the things I love like soccer and salsa dancing.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your concerns are strictly about your appearance, but I want to clarify one more time: are you absolutely certain you've never experienced any obsessive thoughts or compulsions that aren't related to how you look, such as concerns about cleanliness, order, or safety?\n\nPatient: Yes, I'm completely sure that I haven't experienced those kinds of concerns. I've never really thought about things like cleanliness or safety, as my focus has strictly been on my appearance and how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Is there anything else, aside from your appearance, that you feel compelled to think about or check repeatedly, even if it seems minor or insignificant to you?\n\nPatient: No, there really isn't anything else at all that I feel compelled to check or worry about. All of my obsessive thoughts and checking behaviors are strictly focused on my appearance.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where your repetitive checking behaviors or obsessive thoughts were not driven by concerns about your appearance, but perhaps by a fear of something else, like making mistakes or having something bad happen?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think I have those fears about making mistakes or bad things happening. My checking and obsessive thoughts are always completely focused on how I look and trying to hide or fix my appearance, rather than anything else.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where you felt anxious or uncomfortable because of something that wasn't related to your appearance, such as a fear of heights, enclosed spaces, or social situations?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really experienced those kinds of fears like heights or enclosed spaces. My anxiety is almost always tied to how I look and how others might see my appearance.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any time when you had obsessive thoughts or compulsions that were not about your appearance, such as fears of contamination, harm, or symmetry, that you felt compelled to act on, even if it seems minor or insignificant to you?"

It got significantly worse when my soccer teammates started posting high-resolution photos and videos of us online. Now, seeing those images has made me fixate on my crooked face and jawline almost constantly.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your excessive checking and rechecking behaviors are primarily aimed at preventing a specific, catastrophic outcome, such as being ridiculed or rejected by others, or are they more focused on achieving a sense of perfection or symmetry in your appearance?\n\nPatient: It’s actually a mix of both. I’m highly focused on trying to make my face look \"right\" and less crooked, but my ultimate fear is having other people see me looking so \"messed up.\" If I can't get it to look right in the mirror, I end up canceling my plans because I just can't let anyone see me that way.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your behaviors are mainly focused on your appearance concerns, but can you think of any times when you've had repetitive thoughts or urges that aren't related to how you look, such as fears of contamination, harm, or needing things to be perfectly arranged?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never had any of those fears about germs, harm, or needing things to be perfectly arranged. My worries are completely and strictly focused on how crooked my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel emotionally when you're unable to check or fix your appearance, and does it feel like you're trying to reduce anxiety or prevent something bad from happening when you do check?\n\nPatient: If I can't check or fix my appearance, I feel incredibly anxious and uncomfortable because I feel like I absolutely cannot let anyone see me looking \"wrong.\" The checking is my way of trying to reduce that panic and make sure my face looks okay. If I can't get it right, the distress of being seen from a crooked angle is so intense that I'll just cancel my plans and stay home.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your preoccupation with your appearance, such as the perceived crookedness of your face, feels like an intrusive thought that you try to ignore or suppress, or is it more of a voluntary concern that you feel is justified and important to address?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to describe it like that. It just feels incredibly overwhelming and it's really hard to stop thinking about, no matter what I do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that these thoughts about your face being crooked are popping into your mind without you wanting them to, or are they more something you deliberately think about because you're concerned about your appearance?\n\nPatient: They definitely pop into my head automatically without me wanting them to. As soon as I see a photo, a reflection, or even just think about going out, the thoughts about my crooked face and jawline completely take over. I really wish I could stop focusing on them, but they feel totally intrusive and unwanted.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned these thoughts about your face being crooked are intrusive and unwanted. Can you tell me if you've ever experienced any other types of intrusive thoughts or images that aren't related to your appearance, such as violent or disturbing ideas that come into your mind without you wanting them to?\n\nPatient: No, I've never had any violent or disturbing thoughts like that. My intrusive thoughts are strictly focused on my appearance, especially my crooked face and jawline and how I look to other people.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever tried to deliberately ignore or suppress these intrusive thoughts about your appearance, and if so, do you find that trying to ignore them makes them worse or more persistent?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about trying to deliberately ignore or suppress the thoughts, because they usually just take over and feel too overwhelming to push away. Because of that, I'm not really sure if trying to ignore them would make them worse or not.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have control over when these thoughts about your appearance occur, or do they happen completely outside of your control, and are you able to engage in other activities without these thoughts interrupting?\n\nPatient: These thoughts feel completely outside of my control and constantly interrupt my day. It is incredibly hard to focus on other activities because I get stuck checking mirrors or zooming in on photos for hours, which has led to me missing work shifts, canceling plans, and skipping my soccer matches.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where you were able to distract yourself from these intrusive thoughts about your appearance for a significant period, or do they always immediately regain your attention?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a time where I've been able to successfully distract myself from these thoughts. They always seem to take over and pull my attention back immediately, no matter what I'm doing. Even if I try to focus on something else, my mind just goes right back to worrying about how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: You've consistently mentioned that your concerns and behaviors are strictly about your appearance, but can you think of any situation or time where you felt compelled to repeat a behavior or thought that wasn't related to how you look, even if it seems minor or insignificant?\n\nPatient: No, I really can't think of any repetitive behaviors or thoughts that aren't about how I look. All of these habits and worries are strictly tied to my appearance and trying to hide my face.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered that your excessive focus on your appearance might be a symptom of a broader issue, rather than just a concern about how you look, and if so, how do you think that might relate to your overall well-being?\n\nPatient: While the crookedness of my face feels completely real to me, even though my friends say they don't see anything, I am starting to realize that the sheer amount of time and energy I spend worrying about it has become a massive, overwhelming problem of its own. It has severely damaged my well-being by causing me to miss work shifts, avoid my friends, and stop doing the things I love like soccer and salsa dancing.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your concerns are strictly about your appearance, but I want to clarify one more time: are you absolutely certain you've never experienced any obsessive thoughts or compulsions that aren't related to how you look, such as concerns about cleanliness, order, or safety?\n\nPatient: Yes, I'm completely sure that I haven't experienced those kinds of concerns. I've never really thought about things like cleanliness or safety, as my focus has strictly been on my appearance and how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Is there anything else, aside from your appearance, that you feel compelled to think about or check repeatedly, even if it seems minor or insignificant to you?\n\nPatient: No, there really isn't anything else at all that I feel compelled to check or worry about. My checking and obsessive thoughts are always completely focused on how I look and trying to hide or fix my appearance, rather than anything else.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where you felt anxious or uncomfortable because of something that wasn't related to your appearance, such as a fear of heights, enclosed spaces, or social situations?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really experienced those kinds of fears like heights or enclosed spaces. My anxiety is almost always tied to how I look and how others might see my appearance.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any time when you had obsessive thoughts or compulsions that were not about your appearance, such as fears of contamination, harm, or symmetry, that you felt compelled to act on, even if it seems minor or insignificant to you?\n\nPatient: I have never experienced those kinds of thoughts or compulsions. My worries and habits have always been strictly focused on how I look.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your excessive preoccupation with your appearance, specifically the perceived flaws in your face, is something you believe is grounded in reality, or do you have any insight that your concerns might be exaggerated or not entirely based on how you actually look?\n\nPatient: To me, the crookedness of my face and my weird jawline feel completely real and highly visible, especially when I zoom in on photos of myself. Even though my friends constantly tell me they don't see anything wrong at all, I find it incredibly hard to believe them because the asymmetry looks so obvious to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your perception of your face being crooked is an accurate reflection of how you actually look, or do you have any doubt that your concern might be somewhat exaggerated or distorted?\n\nPatient: It feels completely real and obvious to me, so it's really hard to believe my friends when they say they don't see anything wrong. Even though they disagree, I can't help but see it as a major defect that I absolutely have to hide.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your perception of your face being crooked might be distorted or exaggerated, even if it feels completely real to you, and how does that relate to your inability to accept your friends' reassurances that they don't see anything wrong?"

Even if I try to focus on something else, my mind just goes right back to worrying about how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: You've consistently mentioned that your concerns and behaviors are strictly about your appearance, but can you think of any situation or time where you felt compelled to repeat a behavior or thought that wasn't related to how you look, even if it seems minor or insignificant?\n\nPatient: No, I really can't think of any repetitive behaviors or thoughts that aren't about how I look. All of these habits and worries are strictly tied to my appearance and trying to hide my face.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered that your excessive focus on your appearance might be a symptom of a broader issue, rather than just a concern about how you look, and if so, how do you think that might relate to your overall well-being?\n\nPatient: While the crookedness of my face feels completely real to me, even though my friends say they don't see anything, I am starting to realize that the sheer amount of time and energy I spend worrying about it has become a massive, overwhelming problem of its own. It has severely damaged my well-being by causing me to miss work shifts, avoid my friends, and stop doing the things I love like soccer and salsa dancing.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your concerns are strictly about your appearance, but I want to clarify one more time: are you absolutely certain you've never experienced any obsessive thoughts or compulsions that aren't related to how you look, such as concerns about cleanliness, order, or safety?\n\nPatient: Yes, I'm completely sure that I haven't experienced those kinds of concerns. I've never really thought about things like cleanliness or safety, as my focus has strictly been on my appearance and how my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Is there anything else, aside from your appearance, that you feel compelled to think about or check repeatedly, even if it seems minor or insignificant to you?\n\nPatient: No, there really isn't anything else at all that I feel compelled to check or worry about. All of my obsessive thoughts and checking behaviors are strictly focused on my appearance.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where your repetitive checking behaviors or obsessive thoughts were not driven by concerns about your appearance, but perhaps by a fear of something else, like making mistakes or having something bad happen?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think I have those fears about making mistakes or bad things happening. My checking and obsessive thoughts are always completely focused on how I look and trying to hide or fix my appearance, rather than anything else.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where you felt anxious or uncomfortable because of something that wasn't related to your appearance, such as a fear of heights, enclosed spaces, or social situations?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really experienced those kinds of fears like heights or enclosed spaces. I’m highly focused on trying to make my face look \"right\" and less crooked, but my ultimate fear is having other people see me looking so \"messed up.\" If I can't get it to look right in the mirror, I end up canceling my plans because I just can't let anyone see me that way.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your behaviors are mainly focused on your appearance concerns, but can you think of any times when you've had repetitive thoughts or urges that aren't related to how you look, such as fears of contamination, harm, or needing things to be perfectly arranged?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never had any of those fears about germs, harm, or needing things to be perfectly arranged. My worries are completely and strictly focused on how crooked my face looks.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel emotionally when you're unable to check or fix your appearance, and does it feel like you're trying to reduce anxiety or prevent something bad from happening when you do check?\n\nPatient: If I can't check or fix my appearance, I feel incredibly anxious and uncomfortable because I feel like I absolutely cannot let anyone see me looking \"wrong.\" The checking is my way of trying to reduce that panic and make sure my face looks okay. If I can't get it right, the distress of being seen from a crooked angle is so intense that I'll just cancel my plans and stay home.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your preoccupation with your appearance, such as the perceived crookedness of your face, feels like an intrusive thought that you try to ignore or suppress, or is it more of a voluntary concern that you feel is justified and important to address?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to describe it like that. It just feels incredibly overwhelming and it's really hard to stop thinking about, no matter what I do.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that these thoughts about your face being crooked are popping into your mind without you wanting them to, or are they more something you deliberately think about because you're concerned about your appearance?\n\nPatient: They definitely pop into my head automatically without me wanting them to. As soon as I see a photo, a reflection, or even just think about going out, the thoughts about my crooked face and jawline completely take over. My intrusive thoughts are strictly focused on my appearance, especially my crooked face and jawline and how I look to other people.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever tried to deliberately ignore or suppress these intrusive thoughts about your appearance, and if so, do you find that trying to ignore them makes them worse or more persistent?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about trying to deliberately ignore or suppress the thoughts, because they usually just take over and feel too overwhelming to push away. Because of that, I'm not really sure if trying to ignore them would make them worse or not.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have control over when these thoughts about your appearance occur, or do they happen completely outside of your control, and are you able to engage in other activities without these thoughts interrupting?\n\nPatient: These thoughts feel completely outside of my control and constantly interrupt my day. All of these habits and worries are strictly tied to my appearance and trying to hide my face.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever considered that your excessive focus on your appearance might be a symptom of a broader issue, rather than just a concern about how you look, and if so, how do you think that might relate to your overall well-being?\n\nPatient: While the crookedness of my face feels completely real to me, even though my friends say they don't see anything, I am starting to realize that the sheer amount of time and energy I spend worrying about it has become a massive, overwhelming problem of its own. Even though they disagree, I can't help but see it as a major defect that I absolutely have to hide.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your perception of your face being crooked might be distorted or exaggerated, even if it feels completely real to you, and how does that relate to your inability to accept your friends' reassurances that they don't see anything wrong?\n\nPatient: Logically, I guess it's possible my mind is exaggerating it, but to me, the crookedness of my face and jawline is so glaringly obvious that I'll zoom in and pick it apart for hours.
